catalog_quote: [1] No two adjacent syllables within a word are stressed. [2] No word-final syllable is stressed, unless it contains a long vowel. [3] No morpheme-final syllable with a short vowel is stressed, unless it is closed. [4] No more than two unstressed syllables occur in sequence. ... Stress rule 1: primary stress in roots Primary word stress falls on the first syllable which contains a long vowel, as in (d), (e) and (l). In a trisyllabic root without long vowels, if the final syllable is open and a monosyllabic final suffix with a short vowel follows, primary stress falls on the second syllable, as in (f) and (p). Otherwise, if a root contains no long vowels, primary stress falls on the first syllable. audit.reasoning: The deciding quotation is verbatim on thesis p. 53 (page image and text layer held), with the surrounding statements on pp. 52 and 54 also confirmed. The source is the language's only full modern description, by its principal fieldworker, with an explicit ordered-rule account of stress (long vowel = heavy; leftmost long-vowel syllable of the root, else root-initial, with one rule-governed trisyllabic exception), which is exactly what the catalog codes (classification weight, what counts as heavy: CVV, edge=unbounded, domain=word with root-computed primary). Austin 1997 (downloaded) is silent on stress. The only unheld item of note is the 1980 CUP revision of the same work, a low-priority consistency check. no reclassification or grade change indicated.
